_comment: A pattern scanner cannot tell a tool that HUNTS a dangerous construct from
a tool that IS one. Every entry below was triaged by hand and is scoped to
one file plus one rule id. Suppressions are never wildcarded and line
numbers are not pinned, so an unrelated new finding in the same file is
still reported. Re-review these when the file changes.
Honest limitation: these are reviewer judgements, not proofs. A suppressed
path can acquire a genuine defect later without tripping the gate.

suppressions.reason: This module IS a credential-recovery tool. Browser profile and SSH key paths are its declared target inventory, not an exfiltration path introduced by this repo.
The `curl | sh` string appears inside the CI scanner's detection predicate. It is the signature being hunted, not a shell invocation.
Dockerfile `RUN curl ... | sh` is the pattern this hardening module detects and reports. The match is the detection logic.
The pipe-to-shell alternation is part of a regex describing prompt-injection command chaining. It is data in a detection rule.
Sample install command quoted inside a list of known-risky installation patterns used for auditing third-party MCP servers.
Install hint printed as guidance text. No pipe-to-shell execution occurs in this module.
Install hint printed as guidance text. No pipe-to-shell execution occurs in this module.
Credential-path substrings appear inside the audit signature table used to detect malicious MCP tool descriptions.
Indicators searched for in malware samples during triage; the module reads a sample, not a user credential store.
Filesystem paths listed as detection targets for a sensitive-data-exposure audit.
Credential-file guidance text in a key-management playbook. No credential is read by this module.
`id_rsa` appears as a default OUTPUT filename for a key-generation tool, not as a read path.
Destructive commands appear as INDICATOR strings matched against collected shell history during forensics.
Defender-disabling cmdlet appears inside a detection signature used to identify defense evasion in logs.
Defender-disabling cmdlet appears inside a detection signature used to identify defense evasion.
`DROP TABLE` appears inside a log-grep detection signature, not as an executed statement.

`shell=True` appears inside detection regexes that FIND this vulnerability class, not in a subprocess call.
Comment stating that subprocess is NEVER called with shell=True. The rule is documentation asserting the safe form.
`eval()` appears in a finding message describing an unsafe-eval weakness the module reports, not as an eval call.
The PEM header appears in a documentation table describing what to look for, not as key material.
`exec(` and `eval(` are detection regex strings used to identify malicious code in samples under analysis. They are not executed here.
